questions.prompt: Which of these is an absolute location?
choices: Ten paces north of the old oak
Next to the bus stop on Franklin Street
questions.explain: An absolute location is given in a coordinate system that means the same thing to everyone. The others depend on landmarks.

questions.prompt: A GIS needs absolute locations so that layers made by different people line up.
questions.explain: Coordinates that resolve to the same spot for everyone are what let layers be combined.

questions.prompt: Geodesy is the science of measuring the Earth's:
choices: Size, shape, orientation, and gravity field
questions.explain: Geodesy measures the Earth itself: its size, shape, orientation in space, and gravity field.

questions.prompt: Eratosthenes measured a 7.2° shadow angle at Alexandria. Why did that tell him the Earth's circumference?
choices: 7.2° is 1/50 of a circle, so the circumference is 50 times the distance from Alexandria to Syene
7.2° is the tilt of the Earth's axis
The sun is 7.2 times farther than the Moon
Shadows are always 1/50 of a pole's height
questions.explain: The sun's rays are parallel, so the shadow angle equals the angle between the cities at the Earth's center: 1/50 of 360°.

questions.prompt: Why is the Earth modeled as an ellipsoid rather than a sphere?
choices: Its spin makes it bulge at the equator
It is shaped like an egg, pointed at the North Pole
Mountains make it wider than it is tall
questions.explain: The Earth's rotation flattens it at the poles and makes it bulge at the equator.

questions.prompt: The semi-major axis of an ellipsoid is its:
questions.explain: The semi-major axis, a, is the equatorial radius, about 6,378 km for the Earth. The semi-minor axis, b, is the polar radius.

questions.prompt: Flattening is f = (a − ___) / a.
questions.explain: Flattening is the difference between the equatorial radius a and the polar radius b, divided by a.

questions.prompt: The Earth's equatorial radius is about how many kilometers longer than its polar radius?
questions.explain: About 21 km: 6,378 km versus 6,357 km.

questions.prompt: The geoid is:
choices: The surface of equal gravity that best matches mean sea level
A smooth mathematical model of the Earth
questions.explain: The geoid follows gravity and approximates mean sea level. Elevations are measured from it.

questions.prompt: A GPS receiver measures orthometric height, the elevation printed on maps.
questions.explain: GPS measures ellipsoid height, h. Orthometric height, H, is the elevation above the geoid.

questions.prompt: A GPS reports an ellipsoid height h of 250 m where the geoid height N is −32 m. What is the orthometric height H, in meters?
Which equation relates the three heights?
questions.explain: Ellipsoid height equals orthometric height plus geoid height.

questions.prompt: A geodetic datum:
choices: Fixes an ellipsoid's size, shape, and position relative to the Earth
Converts latitude and longitude to x and y
Is a unit of measurement for elevation
Is the same everywhere in the world
questions.explain: A datum pins an ellipsoid to the Earth through a network of control points.

questions.prompt: NAD27 was anchored at a survey station in:
questions.explain: NAD27 used the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid with an origin at Meades Ranch, Kansas.

questions.prompt: Which ellipsoid does NAD83 use?
questions.explain: NAD83 uses GRS 80 and is earth-centered.

questions.prompt: Coordinates from your phone's GPS are almost always in:
questions.explain: GPS uses the WGS84 datum.

questions.prompt: In North America today, WGS84 and NAD83 differ by about 1 to 2 meters.
questions.explain: NAD83 moves with the North American plate; WGS84 is global, so they have drifted apart.

questions.prompt: Two layers that should line up are offset by about 100 m everywhere. What is the most likely cause?
choices: They use different datums, such as NAD27 and NAD83
One layer has too many vertices
The attribute tables use different data types
The layers are drawn in the wrong order
questions.explain: A constant offset is the signature of a datum shift. Fix it with a datum transformation.

questions.prompt: What keeps NAD83 up to date today?
choices: A network of Continuously Operating Reference Stations (CORS)
questions.explain: CORS are permanent GPS stations that run around the clock.

questions.prompt: The prime meridian, chosen in 1884, runs through:
questions.explain: The International Meridian Conference chose Greenwich.

questions.prompt: Latitude is measured:
choices: North and south from the equator
East and west from the prime meridian
questions.explain: Latitude runs from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles.

questions.prompt: Lines of equal latitude are called:
questions.explain: Parallels run east and west. Meridians are lines of equal longitude.

questions.prompt: Where do all meridians meet?
questions.explain: Meridians run from pole to pole and converge at both poles.

questions.prompt: In decimal degrees, Chapel Hill's longitude is written as −79.0558. The minus sign means ___ (one letter).
questions.explain: Negative longitudes are west of Greenwich; negative latitudes are south of the equator.

questions.prompt: Convert 35° 30′ 00″ N to decimal degrees.
Convert 38° 53′ 52″ N to decimal degrees, to four decimal places.
What is −104.54° in degrees, minutes, and seconds?
questions.explain: 0.54 × 60 = 32.4 → 32′; 0.4 × 60 = 24″. Negative longitude is west.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for converting −104.54° to DMS in order.
answer: Multiply the leftover 0.4 by 60 to get 24 seconds
Write W because the longitude is negative
questions.explain: Degrees first, then minutes from the decimal, then seconds from the leftover, then the hemisphere letter.

questions.prompt: About how far is 0.0001° of latitude?
questions.explain: One degree is about 111 km; each decimal place divides that by ten. Four places is about 11 m.

questions.prompt: A phone GPS is accurate to about 3 to 5 m. How many decimal places of a degree are enough?
questions.explain: Five places is about 1 m. More decimals claim precision the phone doesn't have.

questions.prompt: Which distance stays about the same, 111 km, everywhere on Earth?
questions.explain: Parallels are evenly spaced. Meridians converge, so a degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles.

questions.prompt: Which parallel is a great circle?
questions.explain: Only the equator's plane passes through the Earth's center. All meridians are halves of great circles.

questions.prompt: The shortest route between two places on the globe follows a great circle.
questions.explain: That is why airline routes look curved on flat maps.

questions.prompt: The network of parallels and meridians drawn on a map is the:
questions.explain: The graticule shows how a projection bends the globe and helps readers estimate coordinates.

questions.prompt: Plotting longitude as x and latitude as y on an even grid gives:
questions.explain: The Plate Carrée, or equirectangular projection, stretches the map east to west toward the poles.

questions.prompt: Changing a layer's datum can move its points on the ground, while changing its projection only changes how they are drawn on a flat map.
questions.explain: A datum defines where coordinates are on the Earth; a projection flattens them.

questions.prompt: A coordinate system that gives positions in latitude and longitude on a datum is a:
questions.explain: Geographic coordinate systems use degrees, such as WGS84 (EPSG:4326) and NAD83 (EPSG:4269).

questions.prompt: Put the layers of location in order, from the bottom up.
questions.explain: Each layer is built on the one below.
